query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with an FCC matrix, degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing atmospheres is governed by the integrity and adhesion of the protective oxide scale. The hypothesis is that the intrinsic oxide scale formed on the as‐built alloy is prone to spallation, which exposes the underlying matrix to accelerated gas diffusion, internal oxidation (or reduction) and microstructural degradation, ultimately triggering catastrophic failure. A minor reactive element addition (≈0.2 at.% Y) will modify the oxide-scale growth kinetics and adhesion characteristics, thereby stabilizing the scale, reducing gas ingress, and delaying catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA in its as‐built state, characterized by its typical oxide scale formation and surface condition acquired during processing.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled minor reactive element addition (≈0.2 at.% Y) into the HEA composition during processing.
generation.conditions: Expose both the baseline (as‐built, no Y) and Y‐modified alloys to controlled oxidizing (oxygen-rich) and reducing (H2-containing) atmospheres at temperatures between 700 °C and 850 °C for predetermined durations.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation, growth, and adhesion quality of the surface oxide scale – particularly, the enhanced interfacial bonding (e.g., via formation of Y2O3 or interfacial Y-rich compounds) that can inhibit scale spallation.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature gas exposure, the as‐built HEA forms an oxide scale that, if poorly adherent, spalls off and permits rapid gas ingress, leading to localized internal oxidation or reduction and microstructural damage that coalesce into catastrophic cracks. The addition of trace Y promotes the reactive element effect, where Y segregates to the oxide/alloy interface, forming fine precipitates that act as anchor points, thereby enhancing the mechanical integrity and adhesion of the oxide scale. This stabilized scale serves as an effective barrier to gas diffusion and slows the degradation process.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline, Y-modified alloys will develop a more uniform and coherent oxide scale with reduced spallation. Microstructural characterization (using TEM, SEM/EDS, EBSD) will reveal fewer oxide-induced cracks and lower rates of internal gas-assisted oxidation or reduction. Mechanical tests (e.g., residual strength, fracture toughness) are expected to show improved integrity and delayed onset of catastrophic failure.
generation.baseline: The as‐built HEA without Y addition, which is expected to develop a less adherent and more spallation-prone oxide scale under the same exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to conditions of elevated temperature (700–850 °C) and gas compositions that are either oxidizing (oxygen-rich) or reducing (containing H2). Behavior outside these temperature or atmospheric conditions, or under very different exposure times, may involve additional degradation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the quantitative kinetics of oxide scale formation and the uniformity of Y segregation in this multicomponent system. Additionally, interactions between Y addition and the inherent microstructural features from additive manufacturing might have secondary effects on mechanical properties that need further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: (1) the as-built baseline alloy and (2) the same alloy with ≈0.2 at.% Y addition. Expose both sample sets to identical high-temperature conditions (700–850 °C) under controlled oxidizing and reducing atmospheres for varying durations. Post-exposure, conduct detailed microstructural analyses (using TEM, SEM/EDS, and EBSD) and mechanical tests (such as fracture toughness and residual strength measurements).
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and continuity (using cross-sectional SEM/TEM imaging)
Adhesion quality of the oxide scale (e.g., via microscratch or peel tests)
Extent of internal oxidation or reduction (via EDS mapping)
Residual mechanical properties (fracture toughness, hardness, tensile strength)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-modified alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in oxide scale uniformity, adhesion, and resistance to gas-induced internal degradation (as evidenced by comparable oxide spallation, internal oxidation/reduction, and mechanical property degradation to the as-built baseline), then the reactive element mechanism would be falsified as the governing mechanism for degradation in this alloy system.

Beyond conventional alloying, the addition of trace reactive elements, particularly yttrium (Y), has been widely recognized as one of the most effective routes for improving the long-term stability of alumina-forming alloys. This behavior, commonly referred to as the reactive element effect (REE), is generally associated with modified oxide-growth mechanisms, suppressed cation outward diffusion, and enhanced oxide-scale adhesion. According to the dynamic segregation theory [,,], reactive-element ions preferentially segregate to oxide grain boundaries, thereby reducing outward metal-ion diffusion and mitigating growth stress within the scale. In addition, Y-containing oxides may form discrete interfacial anchoring sites, often described as oxide pegs, which mechanically stabilize the scale and inhibit spallation during repeated thermal cycling [,]. Although the REE has been extensively investigated in conventional Ni- and Fe-based superalloys, its interaction with the chemically complex multi-principal-element matrix of HEAs remains insufficiently understood [,]. It is important to note that the superior oxidation resistance of the Innovation Alloy stems from the synergistic effect of both its chemical composition and its unique nanocrystalline microstructure. While the Base and Synergy Alloys were prepared by conventional casting, the Innovation Alloy was fabricated via laser cladding. The rapid solidification inherent in laser cladding leads to significant grain refinement, providing a high density of grain boundaries that act as short-circuit diffusion paths for Al and Cr. This microstructural advantage accelerates the formation of a continuous protective scale. However, the compositional addition of trace Y provides a distinct benefit—the reactive element effect—which enhances the scale/alloy interfacial bonding through the formation of fine Y2O3 particles. This interfacial pinning effect is independent of the grain size and is crucial for preventing scale spallation during thermal exposure. Therefore, the Innovation Alloy represents an optimized system where both process-induced microstructural refinement and alloying-induced chemical stability work in tandem.

proposals.intervention: Minor reactive element addition (e.g., ~0.2 at.% Y) to modify the nature and adhesion of the surface oxide scale
proposals.conditions: Exposure at 700–850 °C in controlled oxidizing (oxygen-rich) and reducing (H2-containing) atmospheres
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation and adherence quality of a protective oxide scale on the HEA surface
proposals.mechanism: Under high-temperature gas exposure, the baseline alloy forms an oxide scale that, if poorly adherent, may spall off. The resulting exposure of the underlying matrix accelerates oxidation (or reduction) and leads to localized weakening (e.g., crack initiation and coalescence). The Y addition is expected to improve the scale's adhesion and modify its growth kinetics, thus delaying or mitigating catastrophic failure.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-built baseline, the Y-modified alloy will show a more coherent and slower-growing oxide scale, reduced spallation or scale delamination, and delayed catastrophic failure under identical gas exposure conditions. Failure surfaces would exhibit fewer oxide-induced cracks.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It tests whether the gas–surface reaction and the integrity of the protective oxide layer govern degradation and eventual catastrophic failure, providing a controlled compositional change to reveal the mechanistic impact.

proposals.intervention: Slight modification of Ti content (e.g., increasing Ti from 0.3 to 0.5 mole fraction) to alter intergranular precipitation kinetics
proposals.conditions: Exposure at elevated temperatures (750–850 °C) in both oxidizing and reducing atmospheres for extended durations
proposals.structural_mediator: The formation of secondary phases or precipitates (e.g., Ti-rich intermetallics or oxide precipitates) especially at grain boundaries
proposals.mechanism: The gas atmosphere (oxidizing or reducing) accelerates diffusion and chemical segregation at grain boundaries. A higher Ti content promotes a higher density of destabilizing precipitates that weaken grain boundary cohesion, triggering intergranular cracking and catastrophic failure. This contrasts with the initial supersaturated solid solution state of the baseline HEA.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The Ti-enriched alloy should exhibit an increased density and size of intergranular precipitates after exposure. Mechanical tests and microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM/EDS) would reveal earlier onset of grain boundary decohesion and lower fracture toughness compared to the baseline composition.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By altering the chemical route to precipitate formation, this approach isolates the role of grain boundary chemical instability induced by gas exposure in dictating degradation and failure.

proposals.intervention: Pre-exposure residual stress relief via controlled annealing treatment (e.g., 600 °C for 2 hours) prior to gas exposure
proposals.conditions: Comparison tests conducted at 750–850 °C under oxidizing or reducing atmospheres, using as-built versus stress-relieved samples
proposals.structural_mediator: The internal residual-stress state (assessed via X-ray diffraction) and its coupling with gas-assisted oxidation or reduction at microstructural defects
proposals.mechanism: Additive manufacturing imparts a high residual stress state that can interact synergistically with gas-induced surface or grain boundary reactions, accelerating oxidation-driven embrittlement and promoting premature crack nucleation. Stress relief is expected to reduce these internal driving forces, thereby moderating the degradation process.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Stress-relieved samples will exhibit slower degradation (e.g., fewer microcracks and less premature oxide formation) and delayed catastrophic failure relative to the as-built baseline. Mechanical testing (e.g., fracture toughness) and microstructural analysis would confirm lower damage accumulation.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach directly tests whether the stored residual elastic energy enhances degradation under gas exposure, allowing for a falsifiable comparison between high-stress and stress-relieved conditions.

proposals.intervention: Controlled modulation of twin density through post-process deformation or annealing treatments to adjust twin boundary populations
proposals.conditions: Expose samples with high versus low twin boundary densities at 750–800 °C in oxidizing atmospheres
proposals.structural_mediator: Density and distribution of deformation twin boundaries and their role as fast diffusion pathways for gas species
proposals.mechanism: Twin boundaries, acting as preferential sites for rapid gas diffusion, can catalyze localized oxidation or reduction at the interfaces. High twin boundary density in the as-built state may lead to localized weakening and microvoid formation that coalesce into catastrophic cracks. Reducing twin density by tailored annealing is expected to slow gas ingress and associated degradation.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Samples with reduced twin density should display significantly lower internal oxidation or gas-induced damage, as evidenced by slower progression of internal cavity formation and higher residual mechanical integrity compared to high-twin-density samples. Transmission electron microscopy and EBSD mapping would show fewer oxidized twin boundaries.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By modulating the microstructural architecture (twin density), this hypothesis tests the role of internal fast diffusion paths in governing the degradation mechanism and eventual catastrophic failure under elevated gas exposures.

decision.rationale: Direction C directly addresses the gas–surface reaction mechanism by modifying the oxide scale’s formation and adhesion. The reactive element effect of adding a small amount of Y is well supported by prior evidence (e.g., PMC13208696) that has demonstrated improved oxide‐scale stability in high-temperature environments. This approach directly tests whether enhanced scale adhesion can mitigate degradation and delay catastrophic failure under both oxidizing and reducing conditions. While the other directions (twin density modulation, residual stress relief, or Ti content modification) are plausible, the Y addition strategy provides a controlled compositional change that isolates the role of the protective scale and its failure (via spallation) as the critical mediator of degradation.
